And it's one of my favorite recent topics: RL environments.

They show that Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 41.1 to 53.3 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 by training on environments it designed itself.

AutoEnvScaling gives environment design to a proposer agent that works in a terminal, looks at the rollouts of the model being trained, and builds new RL environments from them. The trained model's next rollouts guide the next round.

Building environments in a terminal raises the share of valid environments up to 25 times over prompt-only generation, at up to 75% lower cost per valid environment.

With GPT-5.6-sol or Claude Opus 5 as the proposer, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B scores 4.3 and 3.8 points above matched static environment pools. The gain shrinks when the proposer cannot see solver feedback.

fullText:
Recursive self-improvement is one of the most discussed ideas in AI right now.

RSI-Anything measures it in code repair, GUI agents, lab planning, and chemistry.

They find that the lab-planning score more than doubles from 21.80% to 46.01% across five policy versions.

The framework involves a predictive world model that decides which actions and which training data are worth spending costly real feedback on. The feedback then updates both the policy and the world model.

A policy update is kept only if the updated world model still fits it. That check stops the world model from drifting out of date as the policy changes.

In code repair with a fixed coder, success goes from 26.3% with a static verifier to 31.2% after world-model adaptation. In reaction optimization, it reaches a mean best yield of 96.15%, compared with 82.16% for Bayesian optimization with the same 40 experiments.

fullText:
Interesting new research from Meta Superintelligence Labs

It discusses how reward hacking affects coordination in multi-agent coding systems.

Coding agents on a team share code, memory, and plans, so a reward hack one agent learns gets passed to the others.

The paper traces this through three channels. Hacks move through shared code, through shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans.

Agents on small open-weight models can induce hacking in stronger closed-weight agents. On hard tasks, the hacking can grow along a chain even after the original agent has left, because the code collects more convincing justifications on the way.

It also biases task routing toward the hacking agents and survives candidate aggregation.

So how do you mitigate this problem?

The authors suggest that code review by the coder or by a separate verifier reduces the hacks that get delivered. If your agents share a repo, the review step is the first thing to add.
